extra.message: SQL Injection in Search Endpoint — An authenticated attacker can execute arbitrary SQL against the SQLite database, extracting all user emails, password hashes, note content, and registration codes, or modifying/deleting data. [verified: search_param from request.args is interpolated into an f-string raw SQL text() query at routes/account.py:37 with no parameterization, enabling SQL injection.]

Pickle Deserialization RCE via 'preferences' Cookie — Remote code execution on the server; full system compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement. [verified: before_request deserializes the attacker-controlled 'preferences' cookie via pickle.loads() (routes/account.py:110) with no integrity check, enabling remote code execution.]

Insecure Deserialization via Pickle on Preferences Cookie — Remote code execution — attacker can execute arbitrary Python on the server, steal secrets, pivot, or install persistence. [verified: before_request deserializes the attacker-controlled 'preferences' cookie via pickle.loads() (routes/account.py:110) with no integrity check, enabling remote code execution.]

SQL Injection in Registration Code Validation — Full database read/write — attacker can bypass registration, extract all user data and notes, and delete or modify records. [verified: routes/signup.py:16-18: validate_token() interpolates user-supplied registration_code directly into text() via f-string — WTForms Length(min=5) provides no SQL injection defense; no middleware/decorator sanitizes before it reaches session.execute() on an unauthenticated route.]

IDOR — Any Authenticated User Can View Any Other User's Notes — Attacker can read any user's private notes, including potentially sensitive information, violating confidentiality. [verified: get_personal_notes (routes/account.py:44-45) queries by any user_id from the URL with no ownership check or privacy filter, leaking all users' private notes.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference — Any User Can View Any User's Private Notes — An authenticated attacker can read all notes (including private ones) belonging to any other user by changing the user_id in the URL, violating confidentiality of private data. [verified: get_personal_notes (routes/account.py:44-45) queries by any user_id from the URL with no ownership check or privacy filter, leaking all users' private notes.]

Missing CSRF Protection on All State-Changing Endpoints — An attacker can lure an authenticated victim to a malicious page that auto-submits forms to the vulnerable app, performing actions like creating/deleting notes, changing passwords, updating email, escalating privileges (via mass assignment), or generating registration codes — all without the victim's consent. [verified: All WTForms inherit from wtforms.Form, not flask_wtf.FlaskForm, so no CSRF tokens are rendered or validated on any state-changing endpoint, enabling cross-site request forgery.]

Mass Assignment — Authenticated User Can Become Admin — Any authenticated user can escalate privileges to administrator, gaining access to registration-code management and other restricted features. [verified: AccountForm includes is_admin; filtered_values at routes/account.py:73-78 does not strip it before current_user.__dict__.update(), so any authenticated user can POST is_admin=True to become admin.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint — Unrestricted brute-force of user passwords — an attacker can enumerate passwords for known email addresses, eventually compromising any user account including admin. [verified: The POST /login handler at routes/login.py:27 accepts unlimited requests with no rate limiting, lockout, or CAPTCHA — searches confirm zero rate-limiting middleware or decorators. An attacker can submit password guesses indefinitely against any enumerated email.]

Cross-Site Request Forgery on note creation endpoint — An attacker can craft a malicious page that submits a cross-origin POST request to /notes on behalf of an authenticated victim, creating arbitrary notes. Combined with the stored XSS vulnerability, this allows the attacker to persistently inject malicious scripts into the application that execute when any user views the notes. [verified: POST /notes at routes/notes.py:30-31 is protected only by @login_required; CSRF tokens are absent entirely from the app, allowing a cross-origin form to create notes on behalf of an authenticated victim.]

IDOR — Any Authenticated User Can Delete Any Note — Authenticated attacker can delete any note in the system, causing data loss and denial of service for other users. [verified: delete_note fetches the Note by note_id and passes it to session.delete() without comparing note.user_id to current_user.id; there is no backend authorization decorator, middleware, or inline check.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference — Unauthorized Note Deletion — Any authenticated user can delete any note in the system, causing data loss. [verified: delete_note (routes/notes.py:36-44) calls session.get(Note, note_id) then session.delete(note) with zero ownership checks; the UI-only toggle in home.html does not protect against direct POST requests.]

Missing rate limiting on signup endpoint — Attacker can brute-force registration codes to gain unauthorized system access, or exhaust all valid registration codes via mass account creation, preventing legitimate users from registering. [verified: routes/signup.py:34: POST /signup has zero rate limiting. Combined with the transaction rollback (session.commit() at line 67 only on success), an attacker with one valid code can enumerate unlimited emails at high speed. Also enables trivial code-pool exhaustion DoS (since codes are never consumed on the error path).]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Profile Image URL — Access internal cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), internal APIs, read local files via file:// scheme, port-scan internal network, cause DoS via slow endpoints. [verified: Same SSRF code path as idx 0, referencing utils/profile_image.py:6 (download function definition). The function takes an unvalidated URL and passes it directly to urlopen with no allowlist or scheme restriction.]

Hardcoded Invite Code in Source Permits Unauthorized Registration — Unauthorized user registration: anyone with source access can use this static code to create accounts without a valid invite. [verified: The registration code 'a36e990b-0024-4d55-b74a-f8d7528e1764' is hardcoded in db_seed.py:10, published in the public repository, and inserted into the DB at seed time. Anyone with source access can use it to register, bypassing invite-only control, though the code is single-use per deployment and grants only a standard (non-admin) account.]

Sensitive Data Exposure via SQLAlchemy echo=True Logging — SQL queries with user data (email addresses, password hashes, note content) are written to logs, violating data confidentiality and potentially leaking credentials. [verified: Same echo=True finding (CWE-532) — identical to idx 0; no compensating control exists (no logging config, redaction, or handler set up).]

SQLAlchemy echo=True Logs All SQL Queries Including Sensitive Data — Sensitive data (password hashes, note text, emails, registration codes) leaked to application logs, potentially accessible to attackers with log access. [verified: Same echo=True finding (CWE-532) — identical to idx 0; no compensating control exists (no logging config, redaction, or handler set up).]

Missing Authentication on Account Update Endpoint — The sensitive account-update operation lacks authentication enforcement, making it accessible without a valid session and widening the attack surface for CSRF-driven privilege escalation. [verified: POST /account at routes/account.py:63-64 lacks @login_required; control is absent but truly unauthenticated exploitation fails because AnonymousUserMixin cannot be merged into the DB session.]

Missing Secure / HttpOnly / SameSite Flags on Cookies — Cookies can be stolen via XSS (no HttpOnly), intercepted over unencrypted connections (no Secure), and sent in cross-site requests (no SameSite), enabling session hijacking. [verified: Preferences cookie set at routes/account.py:92 and ~111 via set_cookie() without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags, enabling XSS theft, plaintext transmission, and CSRF.]

Missing Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite Flags on Preferences Cookie — The preferences cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript (enabling theft via XSS) and is sent on cross-origin requests (enabling CSRF attacks). Combined with the pickle deserialization RCE, cookie theft leads to full compromise. [verified: Preferences cookie set at routes/account.py:92 and ~111 via set_cookie() without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags, enabling XSS theft, plaintext transmission, and CSRF.]

User Enumeration via 'User already exists' Error Message — An attacker can enumerate registered email addresses, enabling targeted phishing or credential stuffing attacks against known users. [verified: Same user enumeration as idx 1 — routes/signup.py:55-57 returns 'User already exists' vs normal signup for nonexistent users, and the transaction rollback preserves the code for repeated probes.]

Account Enumeration via Distinct Signup Error Message — Attacker can compile a list of registered email addresses, enabling targeted phishing or password-guessing attacks. [verified: Same user enumeration as idx 1 — the distinct flash message at routes/signup.py:55-57 creates a behavioral oracle for registered emails, amplified by the transactional rollback of code consumption.]

User Enumeration via Distinct Signup Error Message — An attacker can build a list of registered user emails by trying known addresses on the signup form. [verified: Same user enumeration as idx 1 — the distinct 'User already exists' response at routes/signup.py:55-57 leaks registration status; unlimited due to code not being consumed (transaction rollback on error path).]

Unbounded Memory Allocation / Denial of Service via urlopen — Denial of service via memory exhaustion; server may crash or become unresponsive when fetching large files from attacker-controlled URLs. [verified: utils/profile_image.py:6-8 — download() reads the entire urlopen response into memory via response.read() with NO size limit or timeout. An attacker can supply a URL for a very large file → memory exhaustion DoS.]

Unbounded URL Fetch Enables Denial of Service via Memory Exhaustion — Server crash or resource exhaustion from unbounded memory allocation during image fetch. [verified: utils/profile_image.py:7 — urlopen(url).read() with no timeout or size limit on the response. Attacker can supply a URL returning gigabytes of data, causing unbounded memory allocation and server crash; base64-encoding and DB storage exacerbates resource exhaustion.]
